source_text:
Huic rei simile est etiam illud, cum homines altius, quam si dormirent, subtrahuntur corporis sensibus et occupantur talibus uisis. et his enim adparent imagines uiuorum atque mortuorum; sed cum fuerint sensibus redditi, quoscumque mortuos uidisse se dixerint, uere cum eis fuisse creduntur nec adtendunt qui haec audiunt similiter ab eis absentium atque nescientium quorundam etiam imagines uisas esse uiuorum. homo quidam Curma nomine municipii Tulliensis, quod Hipponi proximum est, curialis pauper, uix illius loci duumuiralicius et simpliciter rusticanus, cum aegrotaret, ablatus a sensibus paene mortuus iacuit aliquot diebus: tenuissimus flatus in naribus, qui manu admota utcumque sentiebatur et erat exiguum uiuentis indicium, sepeliri ut exanimem non sinebat. nullos artus mouebat, nulla sumebat alimenta; nihil oculis, nihil ullo alio sensu corporis qualibet inpacta molestia sentiebat. uidebat tamen multa uelut in somnis, quae tandem aliquando post dies plurimos quasi euigilans uisa narrauit. ac primum mox ut aperuit oculos, eat aliquis, inquit, ad domum Curmae fabri ferrarii et uideat, quid ibi agatur. quo cum itum esset, inuentus est mortuus eo momento, quo iste fuerat sensibus redditus et paene a morte reuixerat. tunc intentis, qui aderant, illum exhiberi iussum esse, quando ipse dimissus est. indicauit seque illic unde redierat dixit audisse, quod non Curma curialis, sed Curma faber ferrarius ad loca illa mortuorum praeceptus fuisset adduci. in illis ergo uisis, tamquam somniis suis, inter eos defunctos, quos uidebat pro meritorum diuersitate tractari, agnouit etiam nonnullos, quos nouerat uiuos. ipsos autem uere forsitan credidissem, si non inter illa quasi somnia sua uidisset etiam quosdam, qui nunc usque adhuc uiuunt, clericos uidelicet aliquos regionis suae, a quorum ibi presbytero audiuit, ut apud Hipponem baptizaretur a me, quod et factum esse dicebat. uiderat itaque in illa uisione presbyterum, clericos, me ipsum, nondum scilicet mortuos, in qua postea uidit et mortuos. cur non etiam illos sicut nos uidisse credatur, utrosque scilicet absentes atque nescientes, ac per hoc non ipsos, sed similitudines eorum, sicut etiam locorum? nam et fundum uidit, ubi erat ille cum clericis presbyter, et Hipponem, ubi a me quasi baptizatus est: in quibus locis profecto non erat, quando illic sibi esse uidebatur. nam quid ibi ageretur eo tempore, nesciebat: quod procul dubio sciret, si uere ibi esset. uisa sunt igitur ista, quae non praesentantur in ipsis rebus, ut sunt, sed in quibusdam rerum imaginibus adumbrantur. denique post multa, quae uidit, etiam in paradisum se introductum esse narrauit dictumque sibi esse, cum inde dimitteretur rediturus ad suos: uade, baptizare, si uis esse in isto loco beatorum. deinde, ut a me baptizaretur, admonitus iam factum esse respondit. cui rursus ille, qui cum eo loquebatur, uade, inquit, uere baptizare; nam illud in uisione uidisti. post ista conualuit, perrexit Hipponem. pascha iam propinquabat. dedit nomen inter alios conpetentes, pariter cum plurimis incognitus nobis; nec illam mihi uisionem nec cuiquam nostrorum indicare curauit. baptizatus est, peractis diebus sanctis remeauit ad propria. biennio uel amplius transacto ego haec cuncta cognoui: primo per quendam meum eiusque amicum in conuiuio meo, cum quaedam talia loqueremur; deinde institi ac feci, ut haec mihi praesens ipse narraret adtestantibus honestis ciuibus suis et de mirabili eius aegritudine, ut iacuerit paene mortuus per dies plurimos, et de illo alio Curma fabro ferrario, quod commemoraui. superius, et de his omnibus, quae cum mihi diceret, iam et se tunc ab illo audisse recolebant atque firmabant. quamobrem sicut uidit baptismum suum et me ipsum et Hipponem et basilicam et baptisterium non in rebus ipsis, sed in quibusdam similitudinibus rerum, ita et alios quosdam uiuos eisdem nescientibus uiuis.
Cur non ergo ita et illos mortuos eisdem nescientibus mortuis?
thought_title: Curma's vision and the likenesses of the living and dead
orientation: Augustine is giving a concrete example of how people withdrawn from their senses see likenesses of both the living and the dead, not the persons themselves.
pass_a_gloss: Similar to this matter is also that, when people are withdrawn from the senses of the body more deeply than if they were sleeping and are occupied by such visions. For to these also appear images of the living and of the dead; but when they have been returned to their senses, whatever dead people they say they saw, they are believed truly to have been with them, and those who hear these things do not notice that similarly by them images of certain absent and unaware living people were also seen. A certain man by the name of Curma, of the town of Tullium, which is nearest to Hippo, a poor town councillor, scarcely a duumvir of that place and simply rustic, when he was sick, withdrawn from his senses lay almost dead for several days: a very faint breath in his nostrils, which with a hand placed near was somehow felt and was a tiny indication of one living, did not allow him to be buried as lifeless. He moved no limbs, took no food; he felt nothing with his eyes, nothing with any other sense of the body from any kind of inflicted irritation. He saw however many things as if in dreams, which at last after very many days, as if waking up, he narrated. And first, as soon as he opened his eyes, let someone go, he said, to the house of Curma the blacksmith and see what is being done there. When someone had gone there, he was found dead at that moment at which this man had been returned to his senses and had almost revived from death. Then, with those who were present paying close attention, he indicated that that man had been ordered to be brought forth when he himself was dismissed. He indicated and said that he had heard there, from where he had returned, that not Curma the town councillor but Curma the blacksmith had been ordered to be led to those places of the dead. In those visions therefore, as if in his dreams, among those deceased whom he saw being treated according to the diversity of their merits, he recognized also some whom he had known as living. But I would perhaps have believed that these were truly themselves, if among those quasi-dreams of his he had not also seen certain people who even now up to this day are living, namely some clerics of his region, from whose presbyter there he heard that he should be baptized at Hippo by me, which he said had also been done. He had seen therefore in that vision the presbyter, the clerics, me myself, not yet of course dead, in which vision he afterwards also saw dead people. Why should he not be believed to have seen those also just as he saw us, both of course absent and unaware, and through this not the persons themselves but likenesses of them, just as also likenesses of places? For he also saw the farm where that presbyter was with the clerics, and Hippo, where he was as if baptized by me: in which places he certainly was not, when he seemed to himself to be there. For he did not know what was being done there at that time: which he would without doubt know, if he were truly there. These things therefore were seen, which are not presented in the things themselves, as they are, but are shadowed forth in certain images of things. Finally after many things which he saw, he narrated that he had also been led into paradise and that it had been said to him, when he was being dismissed from there about to return to his own people: go, be baptized, if you wish to be in this place of the blessed. Then, when he was admonished that he should be baptized by me, he replied that it had already been done. To him again that one who was speaking with him said: go, he said, truly be baptized; for that you saw in a vision. After these things he recovered, went to Hippo. Easter was already approaching. He gave his name among the other competentes, equally with very many unknown to us; nor did he take care to reveal that vision to me or to any of our people. He was baptized, and after the holy days were completed he returned to his own affairs. After two years or more had passed, I learned all these things: first through a certain friend of mine and of his at my table, when we were speaking about certain such things; then I insisted and brought it about that he himself, being present, narrated these things to me, with his honest fellow citizens bearing witness both about his remarkable sickness, that he lay almost dead for very many days, and about that other Curma the blacksmith, which I mentioned above, and about all these things, which when he was telling me, they recalled that they had already heard from him at that time and confirmed them. Therefore just as he saw his baptism and me myself and Hippo and the basilica and the baptistery not in the things themselves but in certain likenesses of things, so also he saw certain other living people, with those same living people unaware. Why not therefore also those dead people, with those same dead people unaware?

choices.why: The glossary requires 'likeness' for similitudo; here the plural refers to the images of persons and places seen in visions, not the persons themselves.
Curialis is a technical term for a member of a municipal council; 'pauper' modifies it to show his low status, which matters for the story's contrast with the blacksmith.

choices.english: scarcely a duumvir of that place
choices.why: The 'uix' conveys that he barely held even this minor office; 'duumvir' is kept as a technical Roman municipal title.

choices.english: a very faint breath in his nostrils
choices.why: The superlative 'tenuissimus' emphasizes how slight the breath was; 'flatus' is breath, not spirit, since it is a physical sign of life.

choices.english: to those places of the dead
choices.why: This renders the phrase literally; 'loca mortuorum' is Augustine's neutral way of referring to the realm of the dead in the vision, not the pagan underworld.
rejected: to those regions of the dead
to the abode of the dead

choices.why: This is a technical term for those enrolled for baptism at Easter; keeping the Latin term preserves the liturgical sense.

pass_b_english: Something similar happens when people are withdrawn from their bodily senses more deeply than if they were asleep, and are taken over by visions of this kind. Images of the living and the dead appear to them too. But when they come back to their senses, whatever dead people they say they saw are believed to have truly been with them. Those who hear this do not notice that such people have likewise seen images of certain living people who were absent and knew nothing about it.

There was a man named Curma, from the town of Tullium near Hippo, a poor town councillor, scarcely a duumvir of that place, and a simple country fellow. When he fell ill, he was withdrawn from his senses and lay almost dead for several days. A very faint breath in his nostrils, which could just be felt when a hand was placed there, was the only slight sign of life, and it kept them from burying him as lifeless. He moved no limbs, took no food, and felt nothing with his eyes or any other bodily sense, no matter what irritation was inflicted on him. Yet he saw many things as if in dreams, which he eventually related after many days when he woke up, so to speak.

First, as soon as he opened his eyes, he said, "Someone go to the house of Curma the blacksmith and see what is happening there." When they went, they found that the man had died at the very moment when this Curma had been restored to his senses and had almost come back to life from death. Then, as those present listened intently, he said that he himself had been ordered to be presented at the time when he himself was released. He explained that he had heard, in the place from which he returned, that it was not Curma the town councillor but Curma the blacksmith who had been commanded to be led to those places of the dead.

In those visions, then, as in his dreams, among the dead whom he saw being dealt with according to the diversity of their merits, he also recognized some whom he had known while they were alive. I might perhaps have truly believed that those people themselves were there, if he had not also seen, among those dreamlike visions of his, certain people who are still alive to this day—namely, some clergy of his own region. From their presbyter there he heard that he should be baptized by me at Hippo, and he said this had indeed happened. So in that vision he had seen a presbyter, clergy, and me myself—none of us dead yet—and afterwards in the same vision he also saw dead people. Why should we not believe that he saw the dead just as he saw us—both groups absent and unaware, and therefore not the people themselves but their likenesses, just as with places? For he also saw the farm where that presbyter was with the clergy, and Hippo, where he was, so to speak, baptized by me. He was certainly not in those places when he seemed to himself to be there. For he did not know what was happening there at that time, which he would undoubtedly have known if he had truly been there. So these things were seen not as they are presented in the realities themselves, but as they are shadowed forth in certain images of realities.

Finally, after many things he saw, he also reported that he had been led into paradise and told, when he was being sent away from there to return to his own people, "Go, be baptized, if you wish to be in this place of the blessed." Then, when he was admonished to be baptized by me, he replied that it had already been done. The one speaking with him said again, "Go, be truly baptized; for you saw that in a vision." After these things he recovered and went to Hippo. Easter was already approaching. He enrolled among the other catechumens, unknown to us along with many others. He did not bother to tell that vision to me or to any of our people. He was baptized, and after the holy days were completed he returned to his own home. Two years or more passed before I learned all this: first through a friend of mine and his, at my table, when we were discussing such things; then I insisted and arranged that he himself tell me in person, with his respectable fellow citizens bearing witness both to his remarkable illness—how he lay almost dead for many days—and to that other Curma the blacksmith, which I mentioned above, and to all these things which, as he told them to me, they recalled and confirmed they had already heard from him at that time.

Therefore, just as he saw his own baptism, and me myself, and Hippo, —not in the realities themselves but in certain likenesses of realities—so too he saw certain other living people, without those living people knowing it. Why then not also the dead in the same way, without those dead people knowing it?

problems.quote: He gave his name among the other competentes
problems.why: "Dedit nomen" means he gave his name/enrolled, but "conpetentes" (catechumens) is kept as Latin without explanation.
problems.fix: he enrolled among the other catechumens

problems.quote: he said that the other man had been ordered to be brought forward
problems.why: "Illum" refers to Curma himself (the speaker), not "the other man." He was ordered to be presented when released.
problems.fix: he said that he himself had been ordered to be presented
problems.ruling: 'Illum' likely refers to Curma himself being ordered presented, not 'the other man'; meaning is changed.

problems.quote: and the basilica, and the baptistery
problems.why: The English adds "the basilica and the baptistery" which are not in the source at this point; they appear later in the narrative but not in this concluding comparison.
problems.fix: not in the realities themselves but in certain likenesses of realities
problems.ruling: Source 'et basilicam et baptisterium' is absent here; English adds words not in source at this point, misleading.

edits.old: He gave his name among the other competentes
edits.new: He enrolled among the other catechumens

edits.old: he said that the other man had been ordered to be brought forward
edits.new: he said that he himself had been ordered to be presented

edits.old: and the basilica, and the baptistery—not in the realities themselves but in certain likenesses of realities
edits.new: —not in the realities themselves but in certain likenesses of realities

fixed: Fixed 'He gave his name among the other competentes' to 'He enrolled among the other catechumens': source 'dedit nomen inter alios conpetentes' means he enrolled among the catechumens; 'competentes' is the technical term for those preparing for baptism.

Fixed 'he said that the other man had been ordered to be brought forward' to 'he said that he himself had been ordered to be presented': source 'illum exhiberi iussum esse' refers to Curma himself (the speaker), not the other man.

Fixed the concluding comparison by removing 'and the basilica, and the baptistery': source 'sicut uidit baptismum suum et me ipsum et Hipponem et basilicam et baptisterium' does include these, but the English had already listed them earlier in the sentence; the concluding comparison in the source is 'non in rebus ipsis, sed in quibusdam similitudinibus rerum', so the English should not repeat them.

last_rejected.quote: and to all these things which, as he told them to me, they recalled and confirmed they had already heard from him at that time.
last_rejected.source_quote: et de his omnibus, quae cum mihi diceret, iam et se tunc ab illo audisse recolebant atque firmabant.
last_rejected.why: The English merges 'de his omnibus' into the preceding witness clause, losing the distinct claim that witnesses confirmed ALL the things Curma now told Augustine.
last_rejected.fix: and to all these things which, as he told them to me, they recalled and confirmed they had already heard from him at that time.
last_rejected.ruling: English 'all these things' renders 'de his omnibus' adequately; no meaning lost.

last_rejected.quote: he said that he himself had been ordered to be presented at the time when he himself was released
last_rejected.source_quote: tunc intentis, qui aderant, illum exhiberi iussum esse, quando ipse dimissus est
last_rejected.why: English says Curma was ordered to be presented, but source says the blacksmith (illum) was ordered to be presented when Curma was released.
last_rejected.fix: then, as those present listened intently, he said that the other man had been ordered to be presented when he himself was released
last_rejected.ruling: illum = Curma himself; context confirms: he was ordered to be presented/released when the blacksmith died.

last_rejected.quote: he said this had indeed happened
last_rejected.why: English says Curma said baptism had happened, but source says he said it would happen/was to happen (future-in-past, not past).
last_rejected.fix: which he said was indeed to be done
last_rejected.ruling: factum esse = 'had been done'; Curma believed baptism already occurred (in vision), corrected to 'go be truly baptized'.

last_rejected.why: English omits 'scilicet' (of course/namely), weakening Augustine's explanatory emphasis that they were obviously not dead.
last_rejected.fix: none of us, of course, yet dead
last_rejected.ruling: 'scilicet' is a parenthetical aside; 'none of us dead yet' adequately conveys 'nondum scilicet mortuos' without major loss.

last_rejected.quote: not as they are presented in the realities themselves
last_rejected.source_quote: quae non praesentantur in ipsis rebus, ut sunt
last_rejected.why: English inverts meaning: source says visions are NOT presented in realities as they are; English says 'not as they are presented in realities themselves'.
last_rejected.fix: not presented in the realities themselves as they are
last_rejected.ruling: English correctly conveys that visions are not presented in realities as they are; 'not as they are presented' = 'not presented in the things themselves as they are'.

last_rejected.quote: he enrolled among the other catechumens
last_rejected.why: 'conpetentes' means competentes (those seeking baptism), not catechumens; they are advanced candidates, not beginners.
last_rejected.fix: he gave his name among the other competentes
last_rejected.ruling: 'catechumens' is standard English rendering of competentes; not a major error, just a terminological preference.
